title: Mara and the Salt
premise: Marguerite Joubert, once a battle-sworn mercenary of the silent god Veyl, has hidden her fading gift for two decades in Brasse-les-Salines, a city built on salt flats where magic was outlawed after the god's silence broke the old kingdom. When the crown launches a purge of the gifted, Marguerite is betrayed by her oldest friend and forced to flee with a stolen relic: a jar of consecrated salt that can open the Door, the last passage out of a country whose name no longer appears on any map. Pursued by Inquisitor Cassel—a former comrade who believes the god's silence is a test to be survived through obedience—Marguerite crosses drowned villages and salt-blighted fields, learning from ghosts and exiles that Veyl did not die but was devoured by his own faithful. At the Door she must choose between using the salt to escape alone or shattering it to release what remains of the god back into the land; she chooses sacrifice, dying as the Door opens for everyone else, and the epilogue shows the country remembered again under a new name.
about_author: Lior Crane is the pen name of a former archivist who spent a decade cataloguing defunct religious orders before turning to fiction. They write fantasy about faith, forgetting, and the people history leaves behind, and live near a coastline that erodes a little more every year.

chapters.title: Charms for the Fearful
chapters.summary: Marguerite sells a luck-knot to a frightened fisherman in the market of Brasse-les-Salines, hiding her gift behind small, deniable magic. Her POV establishes her careful invisibility, her dead god, and the routine of survival. The emotional beat is weary vigilance—she has made peace with smallness, and the chapter quietly questions whether that peace is real.

chapters.title: The Proclamation
chapters.summary: Criers announce the crown's hunt for the gifted; registration or the pyre. Marguerite watches a neighbor dragged away and realizes her twenty years of caution mean nothing now. Her POV; the beat is dread hardening into resolve as she begins gathering what she'll need to run.

chapters.title: Salt in the Walls
chapters.summary: Marguerite visits Odile, an old hedge-witch living inside the city's salt warehouses, who tells her about the Door—the last way out of a country that officially no longer exists—and the consecrated salt needed to open it. Odile's POV frames the lore. The beat is reluctant hope: escape is possible, but the price is unknown.

chapters.title: An Old Oath
chapters.summary: Marguerite seeks out Tomas Ferreol, her former shield-brother, now a respected guildmaster, believing he might shelter her. He betrays her to the Inquisition instead, weeping as he does it. His POV reveals he genuinely believes surrendering her will save her life. The beat is betrayal wrapped in love.

chapters.title: The Jar of Veyl
chapters.summary: Escaping the raid on Odile's warehouse, Marguerite takes the jar of consecrated salt—the relic that opens the Door—as soldiers burn the building behind her. Odile dies covering her escape. Marguerite's POV; the beat is grief fused with guilt, the first weight of the inheritance she never asked for.

chapters.title: Inquisitor Cassel
chapters.summary: Cassel, Marguerite's former comrade-in-arms, interrogates Tomas and reveals his creed: the god's silence is a trial, and the gifted must be purged so the faithful remain pure enough for Veyl's return. His POV makes him sympathetic and terrifying. The beat is conviction without cruelty, which is worse.

chapters.title: Out Through the Fish Gate
chapters.summary: A smuggler named Perrin agrees to move Marguerite along the coast road for a price she can't yet pay. Their uneasy alliance forms as they slip past checkpoints at dawn. Alternating POVs build wary trust. The beat is fragile partnership between two people who both lie professionally.

chapters.title: The Drowned Village
chapters.summary: They shelter in Sainte-Avoie, flooded when the salt flats were dammed, where the dead still keep their old routines. A ghost-priest recognizes the jar and warns Marguerite that the salt remembers everything it has blessed—including her oath. Her POV; the beat is the past refusing to stay buried.

chapters.title: What the Salt Remembers
chapters.summary: Touching the jar, Marguerite relives her final battle: the moment Veyl went silent mid-prayer, leaving ten thousand sworn soldiers kneeling in the mud. She wakes sobbing while Perrin keeps watch. Her POV deepens the memory theme. The beat is trauma surfacing as literal inheritance.

chapters.title: The Blight Road
chapters.summary: Crossing salt-blighted farmland where nothing grows, they find refugees walking the same direction, all chasing rumors of the Door. Cassel's outriders burn a refugee camp behind them. Perrin's POV shows his cynicism cracking. The beat is horror at scale—this is bigger than one fugitive.

chapters.title: The Choir of Ash
chapters.summary: In a ruined chapel, survivors of the purge have formed a mute congregation who worship the silence itself. Their blind cantor tells Marguerite the heresy: Veyl wasn't abandoned by heaven—he was eaten by his own church, which fed him their prayers until nothing remained. Her POV; the beat is revelation that reframes everything.

chapters.title: Cassel Closes In
chapters.summary: Cassel captures Perrin and offers him freedom for Marguerite's location. Perrin gives up a false trail, buying her two days and sealing his own fate. His POV, written as a confession he expects to die for. The beat is loyalty chosen over self-preservation, echoing the book's central question.

chapters.title: Two Days
chapters.summary: Alone, Marguerite races across the flats toward the Door's coordinates, haunted by visions of Veyl—fragments of a devouring god wearing her old commander's face. Her POV blurs memory and present. The beat is psychological unraveling as the inheritance in the salt speaks through her.

chapters.title: The House That Wasn't Burned
chapters.summary: She shelters in her childhood home, impossibly intact though she watched it burn thirty years ago. Inside, a memory of her mother explains the family's generational bond to the salt: they were its keepers before they were Veyl's. Her POV; the beat is understanding that her whole life of hiding was itself an inheritance.

chapters.title: Reunion at the Wall
chapters.summary: Cassel catches her at the border wall—but instead of arresting her, he asks her to pray with him, revealing he lost his gift the day the god went silent and has been trying to earn it back ever since. Shared POV tension. The beat is two broken believers recognizing each other.

chapters.title: The Door in the Salt
chapters.summary: Guided by the refugees' growing procession, Marguerite reaches the Door: a seam of black glass in the salt flats that only opens for consecrated salt. Hundreds gather behind her. Her POV; the beat is awe curdling into arithmetic—one opening, and the jar holds only enough for one passage.

chapters.title: What We Were Sworn To
chapters.summary: Cassel arrives with his soldiers but cannot order them to fire on unarmed pilgrims; his ranks waver. He and Marguerite argue theology on the salt before the crowd—the book's thematic climax, loyalty versus truth spoken aloud. Dual POV. The beat is honest confrontation between people who loved the same god.

chapters.title: The Devourer Wakes
chapters.summary: When Marguerite pours the first measure of salt, the Door opens—and what crawls through wearing Veyl's shape is the thing that ate him, hungry for the faithful gathered at the threshold. Her POV. The beat is terror and clarity: the god's silence was mercy, and the Door was never an exit—it was a mouth.

chapters.title: The Last Measure
chapters.summary: Marguerite understands the truth the ghost-priest hinted: the salt doesn't open the Door, it feeds whatever waits beyond. She chooses to pour the entire jar into the creature rather than escape, unmaking it and releasing the swallowed fragments of Veyl back into the land. Her POV. The beat is sacrificial resolve—loyalty finally aligned with truth.

chapters.title: Veyl Unbound
chapters.summary: Dying, Marguerite becomes the vessel through which the god's scattered pieces re-enter the world—not as a voice commanding armies, but as quiet presence in salt, rain, and memory. Cassel kneels, not to command this time but to witness. Alternating POV with Cassel carrying her body. The beat is transfiguration: faith restored by being let go.

chapters.title: The Country With a Name Again
chapters.summary: Weeks later, the refugees return to a land where things grow at the edges of the blight, and maps are redrawn with the old kingdom's true name restored. Cassel dissolves the Inquisition and testifies to what he saw. His POV. The beat is mourning braided with renewal—an inheritance passed on.

chapters.title: Charms for the Faithful
chapters.summary: Epilogue: Perrin, alive after all, sets up a market stall selling small charms again—now legal, now blessed. A girl with a faint gift buys a luck-knot, and the salt in the air answers her softly. His POV mirrors chapter one. The beat is quiet grace: the world remade, memory kept, and small magic no longer something to hide.
